# Discussion

## Synthesis of Key Advances, 2016–2024

The period from 2016 to 2024 has witnessed four paradigm shifts that fundamentally altered the conceptual and therapeutic landscape of obesity medicine, representing a discontinuity from prior decades rather than incremental refinement.

The first and most consequential is the reconceptualisation of obesity from a condition attributable to willpower failure to a recognised chronic neurobiological disease driven by dysregulation of the hypothalamic–gut–adipose axis [@Bluher2019Obesity; @Muller2022Antiobesity]. Altered hypothalamic satiety circuits, reduced dopaminergic tone in reward pathways, and impaired leptin and insulin signalling persist even after weight loss, explaining the remarkable difficulty of long-term weight maintenance by volitional effort alone and providing the scientific foundation for pharmacological and surgical interventions that modulate appetite biology directly.

The second paradigm shift is the emergence of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GLP-1/GIP agonists as transformative pharmacotherapy. STEP 1 demonstrated that semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly produced a mean 14.9% weight reduction over 68 weeks in patients with obesity without diabetes [@Wilding2021Once], while SURMOUNT-1 showed tirzepatide 15 mg achieving 20.9% weight loss at 72 weeks [@Jastreboff2022Tirzepatide] — results that, for the first time, approached the 20–25% weight loss typical of sleeve gastrectomy and redefined expectations for pharmacological intervention.

The third paradigm shift is the demonstration that cardiovascular benefit from GLP-1 RA therapy is independent of glucose lowering. The SELECT trial [@Lincoff2023Semaglutide] enrolled 17,604 patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease, obesity, and no diabetes; semaglutide 2.4 mg reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, and non-fatal stroke by 20% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.72–0.90; p < 0.001) over 34.2 months, establishing for the first time that treating obesity itself reduces hard cardiovascular endpoints.

The fourth paradigm shift is the recognition that metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH) constitutes a first-line indication for pharmacotherapy targeting weight loss. Until 2024, no approved pharmacotherapy existed specifically for MASH. The SURMOUNT-NASH trial [@Loomba2024Tirzepatide], a phase 3 randomised controlled trial, demonstrated that tirzepatide 10 mg and 15 mg weekly over 52 weeks achieved MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis in 44.4% and 62.4% of patients, respectively, compared with 9.7% in the placebo group, thereby opening a new therapeutic indication for an agent initially developed for glycaemic control.

## Comparing Treatment Modalities

Across the full spectrum of interventions examined in this review, a consistent hierarchy of efficacy is apparent that tracks closely with the degree of biological mechanism engaged. Lifestyle modification alone — even when delivered with high intensity — achieves a mean weight loss of approximately 5–8% over one year, which, while sufficient to reduce T2D incidence in at-risk individuals, falls short of the 10–15% threshold generally associated with clinically meaningful improvement in cardiometabolic risk factors in patients with established obesity-related disease [@Wadden2020Lifestyle; @LookAHEAD2013Cardiovascular]. The Look AHEAD trial's failure to demonstrate a reduction in cardiovascular events despite sustained 6–8% weight loss at eight years underscored that lifestyle intervention alone is insufficient to modify cardiovascular outcomes in patients with existing T2D and obesity.

Contemporary pharmacotherapy with GLP-1 RAs and the dual GLP-1/GIP agonist tirzepatide bridges a substantial part of the gap between lifestyle intervention and bariatric surgery. Mean weight losses of 15–21% are now routinely achieved in phase 3 trials, with a meaningful proportion of patients achieving 25% or greater weight loss on tirzepatide — outcomes that overlap substantially with the weight loss distribution following sleeve gastrectomy. Bariatric surgery remains the most effective single intervention for severe obesity, producing 50–80% EWL at five years depending on procedure, with the most potent metabolic effects observed with RYGB and BPD-DS [@Schauer2017Bariatric; @Buchwald2004Bariatric]. Crucially, surgical efficacy in achieving T2D remission appears to be partially independent of the degree of weight loss achieved, reflecting the unique neuroendocrine mechanisms operative after intestinal rerouting [@Batterham2016Neuroendocrine]. The most clinically promising strategy emerging from recent literature is the combination of pharmacotherapy and surgical or endoscopic intervention — using GLP-1 RAs to optimise weight loss pre-operatively, reduce operative risk, manage weight regain post-operatively, or treat residual metabolic disease after bariatric procedures.

## Special Populations

Several subpopulations warrant tailored consideration in the context of obesity pharmacotherapy and surgery. Among patients with coexisting T2D, the convergence of glycaemic control and weight loss within single agents is particularly valuable. Tirzepatide in SURMOUNT-2 achieved 15.7% weight loss and a mean HbA1c reduction of 2.4 percentage points in patients with T2D and obesity [@Garvey2023Tirzepatide], while @Schauer2017Bariatric demonstrated that bariatric surgery achieves complete T2D remission in 23–29% of patients even at moderate BMI levels between 27 and 35 kg/m², reinforcing the metabolic indication for surgery below traditional weight thresholds. These complementary data support a framework in which pharmacotherapy and surgery are viewed as synergistic rather than competing strategies within a T2D treatment algorithm.

Patients with MASH represent an emerging priority population for whom no pharmacotherapy was previously approved. SURMOUNT-NASH [@Loomba2024Tirzepatide] establishes tirzepatide as the first agent to demonstrate both MASH resolution and anti-fibrotic efficacy in a phase 3 setting, addressing a condition affecting an estimated 15 million people in the United States and constituting an increasing indication for liver transplantation.

In adolescents, @Kelly2020Randomized demonstrated significant BMI reduction with liraglutide 3.0 mg daily in a phase 3 RCT, while @Weghuber2022Once reported that semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly achieved a 16.1% reduction in BMI versus 0.6% with placebo over 68 weeks — a treatment effect of remarkable magnitude. These data support a multidisciplinary approach integrating pharmacotherapy with behavioural intervention and family-centred care. For elderly patients, sarcopenic obesity creates a distinct challenge: weight loss that preferentially depletes lean mass may worsen physical function and increase fall risk, requiring resistance exercise, protein supplementation, and DEXA-based body composition monitoring alongside pharmacotherapy. The net benefit–risk balance of GLP-1 RAs in adults over 70 remains incompletely characterised and merits dedicated investigation.

## The Weight Regain Challenge

Weight regain following cessation of pharmacotherapy is a defining challenge that reflects the persistence of neurobiological mechanisms defending an elevated body weight set point. The STEP 1 extension study [@Wilding2022Weight] demonstrated that participants who discontinued semaglutide regained approximately two-thirds of lost weight within one year, with near-complete reversal of cardiometabolic improvements. The SURMOUNT-4 trial [@Aronne2024Continued] confirmed this with tirzepatide: continued therapy produced a further 5.5% weight loss, whereas patients switched to placebo regained 14% of body weight over 52 weeks. These data establish that pharmacological weight loss is contingent on continuous drug exposure — analogous to antihypertensive or statin therapy — and that obesity must be managed as a chronic condition requiring chronic treatment.

## Precision Medicine in Obesity

Substantial heterogeneity in individual treatment responses motivates a precision medicine approach to obesity treatment selection. Genetic profiling is beginning to identify stratifying variants: MC4R mutations, the most common monogenic cause of obesity, may predict reduced response to agents acting downstream of the melanocortin pathway; GLP1R variants are associated with differential GLP-1 secretion and potentially variable semaglutide response; and common FTO locus variants are under investigation as risk-prediction biomarkers. Gut microbiome composition influences energy harvest, bile acid metabolism, and GLP-1 secretion in ways that likely modulate treatment response to both pharmacological and surgical interventions. Psychobehavioural phenotyping — distinguishing hedonic or emotional eating from hyperphagia driven by deficient satiety signalling — may also guide pharmacotherapy selection, as these subtypes may respond differentially to agents targeting reward circuitry versus those primarily suppressing meal-driven appetite.

## Health Equity and Access

The transformative efficacy of contemporary obesity pharmacotherapy is accompanied by a stark disparity in access that threatens to widen existing health inequities. Tirzepatide and high-dose semaglutide carry list prices of approximately $1,000–1,500 per month in the United States without insurance coverage, placing them out of reach for the populations bearing the highest obesity burden — those in lower socioeconomic strata, racial and ethnic minorities, and residents of low- and middle-income countries. Insurance coverage for anti-obesity medications remains inconsistent: as of 2024, Medicare did not cover GLP-1 RAs for obesity without T2D, and many state Medicaid programmes similarly exclude these agents, meaning that access is effectively determined by employer-sponsored insurance generosity rather than clinical need. Globally, these agents are approved and available in a fraction of the countries where obesity prevalence is highest. The timeline to generic availability for semaglutide and tirzepatide — likely a decade or more given patent portfolios — means that access barriers will persist for the foreseeable future unless policy interventions mandate coverage or accelerate entry of lower-cost alternatives.

## Future Directions

The pharmacological pipeline beyond the current generation of GLP-1 RAs and dual agonists is exceptionally active. Retatrutide, a triple agonist targeting GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors simultaneously, produced a mean body weight reduction of 24.2% at 48 weeks in a phase 2 trial [@Jastreboff2023Triple] — a magnitude that exceeds any previous pharmacological result and approaches outcomes seen with RYGB in selected patients. Phase 3 trials of retatrutide are underway and, if confirmed, its approval would represent another step-change in the pharmacological management of severe obesity. Oral semaglutide has been approved for the treatment of T2D and is under regulatory evaluation for the obesity indication, which would substantially reduce the barrier to treatment initiation associated with subcutaneous injection. Amylin-based strategies, including the long-acting amylin analogue cagrilintide, are being evaluated in combination with semaglutide (CagriSema), with phase 2 data suggesting weight losses approaching 15% — additional options that may prove valuable in patients who experience adverse effects with or partial responses to GLP-1 RA monotherapy. Melanocortin 4 receptor agonists (setmelanotide) have established proof of concept in rare monogenic obesity syndromes and are being explored in broader polygenic obesity. At the preclinical stage, gene therapy strategies targeting FTO and MC4R dysregulation offer the theoretical possibility of modifying the molecular set point for body weight, though the translation of these approaches to clinical application remains many years distant. In the endoscopic domain, continued refinement of ESG technique, development of more durable intragastric devices, and expansion of the endobariatric evidence base are expected to establish this category as a meaningful tier in the stepped care model of obesity management.

## Strengths and Limitations of This Review

This systematic review was designed to minimise the methodological limitations that commonly affect evidence synthesis in rapidly evolving clinical fields. Strengths include a comprehensive multi-database search strategy spanning PubMed with quality filtering by CiteScore and SJR thresholds, a structured two-stage screening process applying pre-specified inclusion and exclusion criteria, independent validation of all included DOIs via the doi.org resolution API, and examination of diverse clinical endpoints spanning weight loss, glycaemic outcomes, cardiovascular events, and procedure-specific adverse events across a broad range of study designs. The review explicitly integrates data from lifestyle, pharmacological, and surgical literatures to enable cross-modality comparisons that are absent from single-domain reviews.

Limitations must nonetheless be acknowledged. Network access restrictions during the search process were primarily limited to PubMed-indexed literature, with reduced access to Embase and Scopus for portions of the search, which may have introduced partial database bias despite efforts to cross-reference key findings. The search period of 2016–2024, while capturing the most clinically relevant contemporary evidence, necessarily excludes pivotal earlier trials — including the SOS study's initial reports and foundational pharmacotherapy RCTs — that provide essential context; these were incorporated by design as background citations rather than systematic inclusions. Publication bias remains an inherent limitation of any systematic review: positive trial results are more likely to be published, more likely to appear in higher-impact journals accessible through quality filters, and more likely to be cited by subsequent literature. Finally, this is a rapidly evolving field in which major phase 3 trial data for emerging agents continue to emerge; results published after the search date cutoff are not represented, and the comparative landscape of obesity pharmacotherapy may shift materially within the near-term horizon.

## Conclusions

Obesity has emerged from decades of therapeutic neglect to become one of the most actively researched conditions in contemporary medicine, and the period from 2016 to 2024 has delivered advances of a magnitude and pace rarely seen in any therapeutic area. The central message of this systematic review is that obesity is a complex, chronic, neurobiologically mediated disease for which effective treatments now exist across a broad spectrum of severity and patient circumstance. GLP-1 receptor agonists and the dual GLP-1/GIP agonist tirzepatide have achieved pharmacological weight reductions — 15–21% of body weight in pivotal trials — that rival those achieved by bariatric sleeve gastrectomy in selected patients, while the SELECT trial has established cardiovascular outcome benefit independent of glycaemic effect. Bariatric surgery remains the most potent and metabolically transformative modality available for severe obesity with comorbid T2D, and its superiority in achieving T2D remission over intensive medical therapy has been definitively confirmed in multiple randomised controlled trials. The challenge ahead is not primarily one of efficacy — the treatments now available are effective — but of access, durability, and personalisation. Ensuring that the most effective interventions reach the patients with the greatest need, managing the chronic nature of the disease with continuous long-term treatment strategies, and developing precision tools to match individuals to the most appropriate therapy represent the defining clinical and scientific priorities for the next decade of obesity medicine.
